items.stem: Which of these tasks is the best fit for a general AI assistant?

options.text: Finding out what a competitor announced this morning.
options.feedback: Poor fit. Recent events may be missing from what the assistant learned, and it may invent an answer rather than admit it does not know.

options.text: Turning your rough meeting notes into a tidy summary with action points.
options.feedback: Correct. Summarising and reformatting text you supply is a core strength, and you can check the result against your own notes.

options.text: Calculating the exact VAT owed across 300 invoices.
options.feedback: Poor fit. Assistants are unreliable at arithmetic, and an error across 300 invoices would be costly. Use a spreadsheet or the finance system.

options.text: Telling you how many unread emails are in your manager's inbox.
options.feedback: Poor fit. The assistant cannot see anything it has not been given access to, so any number would be invented.

items.explanation: Assistants are strong at working with text you give them: drafting, summarising, reformatting and brainstorming. They are weak at maths, recent events and anything they cannot see.

items.stem: In the prompt below, which phrase supplies the Context? You are a recruiter. Write a job advert for a payroll officer. Our team is small and values flexible hours. Use five bullet points.

options.text: You are a recruiter.
options.feedback: That is the Role. It tells the assistant who to act as, not the background to the request.

options.text: Write a job advert for a payroll officer.
options.feedback: That is the Task. It names the action and the deliverable.

options.text: Use five bullet points.
options.feedback: That is the Format. It sets the shape of the output.

options.text: Our team is small and values flexible hours.
options.feedback: Correct. This is background the assistant could not know, and it shapes what the advert should stress.

items.explanation: Context is the background and constraints: the audience, the goal, the situation and anything to avoid. Here it is the detail about the team.

items.stem: A colleague types: write a message about the system outage. Which additions would most improve the prompt? Select all that apply.

options.text: Add: you are an IT service desk lead writing to non-technical staff.
options.feedback: Yes. A Role sets the voice and level of detail for the reader.

options.text: Add: the outage lasted two hours, is now fixed, and staff need to know if any work was lost.
options.feedback: Yes. Context gives the facts and the reader's main concern, so the assistant does not have to guess.

options.text: Add: please, this is really important.
options.feedback: Not helpful. Politeness is fine, but it gives the assistant no information about what to write.

options.text: Add: under 100 words with a clear subject line.
options.feedback: Yes. Format controls length and layout, which saves editing time.

items.explanation: The original prompt has only a vague Task. Adding Role, Context and Format gives the assistant what it needs; urgency words add nothing it can use.

items.stem: An assistant gives you a statistic and a link to a source. What is the right way to verify it?

options.text: Open the link and find the exact figure on the page.
options.feedback: Correct. Only the source itself confirms the figure. Assistants can cite real pages that say something different, or links that do not exist.

options.text: Ask the assistant whether it is sure.
options.feedback: Not enough. The assistant may simply repeat or rephrase the same claim with equal confidence.

options.text: Check that the link looks like a real website address.
options.feedback: Not enough. A plausible address can be invented, and a real page may not contain the figure.

options.text: Accept it, because the answer included a source.
options.feedback: Risky. A cited source is a lead to check, not proof.

items.explanation: Verification means comparing the claim with a source you have opened yourself. Confidence and plausible links are not evidence.

items.stem: Put these steps for checking an AI-drafted customer email in the best order before you send it.

items.text: Read the whole draft to check it answers what the customer actually asked.
Check every name, number, date and link against the customer record or policy.
Adjust the tone and remove anything you would not say yourself.
Do a final read as the customer would see it, then send.

items.explanation: Start with the big question of whether the draft answers the request, then confirm facts, then polish tone. A final read catches anything the edits introduced.

items.stem: Which of these is safe to paste into a free public AI tool your organisation has not approved?

options.text: A spreadsheet of customer names, email addresses and order totals.
options.feedback: Unsafe. This is personal data and customer records, which must never go into an unapproved tool.

options.text: The draft quarterly results before they are announced.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Unpublished financials are confidential and could be market-sensitive.

options.text: A request to suggest five titles for a public blog post about recycling at work.
options.feedback: Correct. It contains no personal, customer, financial, legal or credential data, and the topic is already public.

options.text: The login details for a shared supplier portal, so it can help you navigate it.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Passwords and credentials must never be shared with any AI tool.

items.explanation: Public, non-identifying material is fine. Personal data, customer records, credentials, confidential financials and legal matters stay out of unapproved tools.

items.stem: You want help replying to an angry complaint from a named customer. Which steps keep the request safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use your organisation's approved enterprise assistant.
options.feedback: Yes. Approved tools have agreed rules on how your data is stored and used.

options.text: Replace the customer's name, account number and address with placeholders.
options.feedback: Yes. Anonymising means the draft can be written without revealing who the customer is.

options.text: Describe the complaint in general terms instead of pasting the full email thread.
options.feedback: Yes. A short description gives the assistant enough context without copying personal details.

options.text: Paste the full thread into a public chatbot, then delete the chat.
options.feedback: No. Deleting your copy does not undo sending the data, which may already be stored by the provider.

items.explanation: Use the approved tool, share the minimum and remove identifying details. Deleting a chat afterwards does not reverse a disclosure.

items.stem: Your finance team wants to start using an AI assistant. Which task is the best first use case?

options.text: Deciding which suppliers to stop paying when cash is tight.
options.feedback: Poor choice. This is a high-stakes business decision with legal and relationship consequences. A person must make it.

options.text: Interpreting a new tax regulation for the annual return.
options.feedback: Poor choice. This is specialist legal and tax advice that the team may not be able to check, and errors carry penalties.

options.text: Calculating month-end accruals from the ledger.
options.feedback: Poor choice. Assistants are unreliable at maths, and the ledger system or a spreadsheet does this accurately.

options.text: Drafting standard reminder emails for routine late payments.
options.feedback: Correct. It is frequent, low risk and easy for the team to check, and they know exactly what a good reminder looks like.

items.explanation: Good first use cases are high volume, low risk, easy to verify and within your expertise. Decisions, specialist advice and calculations do not qualify.

items.stem: An AI-drafted report you sent to a client contained a wrong figure. The client complains. Who is accountable?

options.text: The company that makes the AI assistant.
options.feedback: No. The supplier provides a tool. The work you send is yours.

options.text: You, as the person who sent the report.
options.feedback: Correct. You chose to send it, so you own the error. Apologise, correct it and tighten your checking.

options.text: Nobody, because AI errors are expected.
options.feedback: No. Expecting errors is the reason you check. It does not remove responsibility.

options.text: The IT team, because they approved the tool.
options.feedback: No. Approving a tool means it is safe to use, not that its output is correct.

items.explanation: The assistant drafts and you decide. Whoever sends, signs or acts on the work is accountable for it.

items.stem: An assistant drafts a reply that would commit your company to a refund well above your approval limit. Put the steps in the right order.

items.text: Hold the draft rather than sending it.
Send the draft to your manager, noting that AI wrote the first version and the refund exceeds your limit.
Update the reply to match the decision your manager makes.
Send the approved reply under your own name.

items.explanation: High stakes mean escalation before sending. Disclose AI use to the reviewer, apply their decision, and then you send and own the final reply.
